title: Integer division
summary: Dividing an integer by an integer drops the fraction on SQLite and PostgreSQL; MySQL and MariaDB keep it.
detail: SQLite and PostgreSQL give an integer result when both sides of / are integers, so 7 / 2 is 3. MySQL and MariaDB always divide as decimals and answer 3.5000. Averages written as SUM(x) / COUNT(*) are where this usually bites: the sum of an integer column is an integer on SQLite and PostgreSQL, so the average loses its fraction there.
advice: Multiply one side by 1.0 for the fraction and round it to the places you need (see decimal-division): ROUND(7 * 1.0 / 2, 2) is 3.5 on every engine. For a whole number on every engine, take the remainder off first: (7 - 7 % 2) / 2.
example: SELECT 7 / 2
rewrite: SELECT ROUND(7 * 1.0 / 2, 2)

title: Dividing decimals
summary: 80.50 / 3 is 26.833333 on MySQL and MariaDB, 26.8333333333333333 on PostgreSQL and a floating point number on SQLite.
detail: MySQL and MariaDB give the result of a decimal division four more decimal places than the dividend has (the div_precision_increment setting) and cut it there. PostgreSQL keeps at least 16 significant digits, and SQLite divides as floating point numbers. Shares of an amount, prices per unit and AVG of a DECIMAL column then differ in the last digits, and sums of them by a cent here and there.
advice: Round on purpose to the places you need: ROUND(80.50 / 3, 2) is 26.83 on all four engines.
example: SELECT 80.50 / 3
rewrite: SELECT ROUND(80.50 / 3, 2)

title: || joins text on some engines only
summary: || joins text on SQLite and PostgreSQL. On MySQL and MariaDB it means OR, so 'a' || 'b' is 0.
detail: The SQL standard joins strings with ||, and SQLite and PostgreSQL follow it. MySQL and MariaDB read || as a logical OR unless the server runs in the PIPES_AS_CONCAT mode, so both strings are turned into numbers and the answer is 0. The warnings they give for it seldom reach the application.
advice: Use CONCAT(a, b), which all four engines have (SQLite from version 3.44). CONCAT treats NULL differently on different engines; see concat-null.
example: SELECT 'a' || 'b'
rewrite: SELECT CONCAT('a', 'b')

title: CONCAT with a NULL argument
summary: CONCAT skips NULL arguments on SQLite and PostgreSQL. On MySQL and MariaDB one NULL makes the whole result NULL.
detail: A person without a last name comes out as 'Ann ' on SQLite and PostgreSQL and as NULL on MySQL and MariaDB, so a list of names quietly loses entries there. CONCAT_WS skips NULL arguments on all four engines.
advice: Wrap every argument that can be NULL in COALESCE(x, '').
setup:
CREATE TABLE people (first_name VARCHAR(20), last_name VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO people VALUES ('Ann', NULL)
example: SELECT CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name) FROM people
rewrite: SELECT CONCAT(COALESCE(first_name, ''), ' ', COALESCE(last_name, '')) FROM people

title: Text comparisons and letter case
summary: MySQL and MariaDB compare text without regard to letter case or accents by default; SQLite and PostgreSQL compare it exactly.
detail: The default collations of MySQL and MariaDB ignore case and accents, so 'abc' = 'ABC' and 'e' = 'é' are true there and false on SQLite and PostgreSQL. The same goes for joins, GROUP BY, DISTINCT and unique keys: two e-mail addresses that differ only in case are one value on MySQL and two elsewhere. Whether an answer changes depends on the data, so lint reports this as information.
advice: Compare LOWER(a) = LOWER(b) where case should not matter, and store values in one case. No form makes MySQL compare exactly without naming a collation, and collation names differ on every engine.
example: SELECT 'abc' = 'ABC'
rewrite: SELECT LOWER('abc') = LOWER('ABC')

title: LIKE and letter case
summary: LIKE ignores letter case on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB and respects it on PostgreSQL.
detail: SQLite's LIKE ignores case for the letters A to Z only. MySQL and MariaDB follow the collation, which ignores case by default. PostgreSQL's LIKE is exact; its ILIKE ignores case, and exists on PostgreSQL only.
advice: Write LOWER(x) LIKE LOWER(pattern), or a pattern that is already in lower case, to ignore case on all four.
example: SELECT 'abc' LIKE 'ABC'
rewrite: SELECT LOWER('abc') LIKE LOWER('ABC')

title: Comparing text with a number
summary: Comparing a text column with a number matches text like 'abc' to 0 on MySQL and MariaDB, matches nothing on SQLite and fails on PostgreSQL.
detail: MySQL and MariaDB turn the text into a number, and text that does not start with digits becomes 0, so WHERE code = 0 finds every code like 'abc'. SQLite compares the number as text and finds nothing. PostgreSQL refuses to compare character varying with integer. '1' = 1 trips over the same thing in another way: false on SQLite, true on the other three.
advice: Compare like with like: quote the number when the column holds text (code = '0'), or convert one side with CAST.
setup:
CREATE TABLE items (code VARCHAR(10));
INSERT INTO items VALUES ('abc')
example: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM items WHERE code = 0
rewrite: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM items WHERE code = '0'

items.name: text column = number
items.setup:
CREATE TABLE items (code VARCHAR(10), n INTEGER);
INSERT INTO items VALUES ('abc', 0)
items.probe: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM items WHERE code = 0
items.message: {what} compares a text column with a number: MySQL and MariaDB turn the text into a number, so 'abc' matches 0, SQLite compares it as text and finds nothing, and PostgreSQL refuses it.
{what} compares text with a number: false on SQLite, true on PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB.

items.name: 'abc' = number
items.setup:
CREATE TABLE scores (n INTEGER);
INSERT INTO scores VALUES (0)
items.probe: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM scores WHERE n = 'abc'
items.message: {what} compares text that is no number with a number: PostgreSQL refuses it, MySQL and MariaDB read the text as 0, and SQLite finds no match.

title: Double quotes
summary: Double quotes name a column on SQLite and PostgreSQL. On MySQL and MariaDB they make a string, so SELECT "name" returns the word name.
detail: Standard SQL quotes names with double quotes, and SQLite and PostgreSQL follow it. MySQL and MariaDB read "..." like '...' unless the ANSI_QUOTES mode is on: the query still runs and returns the same text on every row. SQLite also turns a double-quoted word into a string when no column has that name.
advice: Use single quotes for text. For names, use plain lower-case names that are not keywords: that is the one form all four engines read the same way.
setup:
CREATE TABLE people (name VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO people VALUES ('Ann')
example: SELECT "name" FROM people
rewrite: SELECT name FROM people

title: Where NULL sorts
summary: SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB put NULL first in ascending order; PostgreSQL puts it last.
detail: The standard leaves the place of NULL in ORDER BY to the engine. PostgreSQL treats NULL as larger than every value, the others as smaller, and descending order turns both around. Pages of results, top-ten lists and window functions such as ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY x) all change when the column holds NULL.
advice: Sort on x IS NULL first: ORDER BY x IS NULL, x puts NULL last on every engine, and ORDER BY x IS NOT NULL, x puts it first. NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST do not work on MySQL and MariaDB.
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (NULL), (2)
example: SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x
rewrite: SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x IS NULL, x

title: Columns missing from GROUP BY
summary: A selected column that is neither grouped nor aggregated takes its value from any row of the group on SQLite and MariaDB; PostgreSQL and MySQL refuse the query.
detail: SELECT a, b FROM t GROUP BY a asks for one b per group without saying which. SQLite and MariaDB pick one (MariaDB's default mode leaves out ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY). PostgreSQL and MySQL stop with an error, unless the grouped column is the table's primary key, which fixes every other column of that table.
advice: Add the column to GROUP BY, or say which value you want with an aggregate such as MAX(b).
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 1), (1, 2)
example: SELECT a, b FROM t GROUP BY a
rewrite: SELECT a, MAX(b) FROM t GROUP BY a

title: CAST to text
summary: CAST(123 AS CHAR) is '1' on PostgreSQL, where CHAR means CHAR(1), and '123' elsewhere; no text type works in CAST on all four engines.
detail: PostgreSQL reads CHAR without a length as CHAR(1) and cuts the value to fit. With a length, CHAR(10), it pads the value with spaces. MySQL accepts CHAR in CAST but neither VARCHAR nor TEXT, and MariaDB accepts VARCHAR but not TEXT.
advice: CONCAT(x) with one argument turns a value into text on all four engines (SQLite from version 3.44).
example: SELECT CAST(123 AS CHAR)
rewrite: SELECT CONCAT(123)

items.name: CHAR
items.message: CAST(x AS CHAR) keeps one character on PostgreSQL, where CHAR means CHAR(1).

items.name: CHAR(n)
items.message: CAST(x AS CHAR(n)) pads the value with spaces to n characters on PostgreSQL.

title: CAST to an integer or a decimal
summary: CAST(5.7 AS INTEGER) is 5 on SQLite, 6 on PostgreSQL and MariaDB, and an error on MySQL, which wants SIGNED.
detail: SQLite drops the fraction and PostgreSQL and MariaDB round it. MySQL takes only SIGNED and UNSIGNED as integer types in CAST, and PostgreSQL refuses both. Decimals differ as well: SQLite ignores the scale of CAST(x AS DECIMAL(10, 1)) and keeps every digit, and MySQL and MariaDB read DECIMAL without a precision as DECIMAL(10, 0), a whole number.
advice: Round on purpose with ROUND(x) or ROUND(x, digits), which every engine has.
example: SELECT CAST(5.7 AS INTEGER)
rewrite: SELECT ROUND(5.7)

items.name: INTEGER
items.message: MySQL refuses CAST(x AS {what}), and SQLite drops the fraction where PostgreSQL and MariaDB round it.

items.name: INT
items.message: MySQL refuses CAST(x AS {what}), and SQLite drops the fraction where PostgreSQL and MariaDB round it.

items.name: SIGNED
items.message: PostgreSQL refuses CAST(x AS {what}), and SQLite keeps the fraction.

items.name: UNSIGNED
items.message: PostgreSQL refuses CAST(x AS {what}), and SQLite keeps the fraction.

items.name: DECIMAL
items.message: CAST(x AS DECIMAL) rounds to a whole number on MySQL and MariaDB (DECIMAL(10, 0)) and keeps every digit on PostgreSQL and SQLite.

items.name: DECIMAL(p, s)
items.message: SQLite ignores the scale of DECIMAL(p, s) and keeps every digit; the other engines round.

title: CAST to a date
summary: SQLite has no date type: CAST('2024-05-06' AS DATE) is the number 2024 there and a date on the other engines.
detail: SQLite keeps dates as text or numbers and reads a CAST to DATE, DATETIME or TIMESTAMP as a conversion to a number, which keeps only the leading digits. MySQL and MariaDB also refuse CAST(x AS TIMESTAMP), and PostgreSQL refuses DATETIME.
advice: DATE(x) gives a date on PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB and ISO text (2024-05-06) on SQLite, which sorts and compares the same way.
example: SELECT CAST('2024-05-06' AS DATE)
rewrite: SELECT DATE('2024-05-06')

items.name: TIME
items.message: SQLite has no time type: CAST(x AS TIME) turns the value into a number there.

items.name: DATETIME
items.message: PostgreSQL refuses CAST(x AS DATETIME), and SQLite turns the value into a number.

items.name: TIMESTAMP
items.message: MySQL and MariaDB refuse CAST(x AS TIMESTAMP), and SQLite turns the value into a number.

title: Adding numbers to dates
summary: A date plus 1 is the next day on PostgreSQL, the number 20240132 on MySQL and MariaDB, and 2025 on SQLite.
detail: MySQL and MariaDB turn the date into the number 20240131 and add 1. SQLite turns the text into the number 2024. PostgreSQL adds a day. Subtracting two dates goes the same way: PostgreSQL counts days and MySQL and MariaDB subtract the numbers. INTERVAL arithmetic works on PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, with different result types, and SQLite has no INTERVAL. PostgreSQL's usual INTERVAL '1 day', with the unit inside the quotes, works on PostgreSQL only.
advice: No date arithmetic reads the same on all four engines. Use date(d, '+1 day') on SQLite and d + INTERVAL '1' DAY on the other three, or do the arithmetic in the application.
example: SELECT CAST('2024-01-31' AS DATE) + 1

items.name: INTERVAL
items.probe: SELECT CAST('2024-01-31' AS DATE) + INTERVAL '1' DAY
items.message: SQLite has no INTERVAL, and the other engines give the result different types.

items.name: INTERVAL 'n unit'
items.probe: SELECT CAST('2024-01-31' AS DATE) + INTERVAL '1 day'
items.message: INTERVAL '1 day', with the unit inside the quotes, works on PostgreSQL only: SQLite has no INTERVAL, and MySQL and MariaDB want the unit outside them, INTERVAL '1' DAY.

title: Division by zero
summary: 1 / 0 is NULL on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB and an error on PostgreSQL.
detail: PostgreSQL stops the whole statement. SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB answer NULL, MySQL and MariaDB with a warning, and in INSERT and UPDATE with an error when the strict mode includes ERROR_FOR_DIVISION_BY_ZERO (the default). The remainder operator % behaves the same way.
advice: Divide by NULLIF(d, 0): every engine then answers NULL when d is 0.
example: SELECT 1 / 0
rewrite: SELECT 1 / NULLIF(0, 0)

title: DECIMAL on SQLite
summary: SQLite stores DECIMAL and NUMERIC values as floating point numbers, so sums of prices pick up rounding errors the other engines do not have.
detail: PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB keep DECIMAL values exact, so the sum of 0.1 and 0.2 equals 0.3 there. SQLite has no exact decimal type: it stores 0.1 as the nearest binary fraction, the sum is 0.30000000000000004, and the comparison is false.
advice: Compare rounded values, ROUND(x, 2) = 0.3, or keep amounts as integers in the smallest unit, such as cents.
setup:
CREATE TABLE prices (price DECIMAL(10, 2));
INSERT INTO prices VALUES (0.1), (0.2)
example: SELECT SUM(price) = 0.3 FROM prices
rewrite: SELECT ROUND(SUM(price), 2) = 0.3 FROM prices

title: REAL and FLOAT precision
summary: REAL on PostgreSQL and FLOAT on MySQL and MariaDB are 4-byte floats, so 1.23456789 comes back as 1.2345679 or 1.23457; elsewhere both names mean an 8-byte float, which keeps about 15 digits.
detail: PostgreSQL's REAL is a 4-byte float, and so is FLOAT on MySQL and MariaDB, while the other engines store 8 bytes for the same name. 1.23456789 comes back as 1.2345679 or 1.23457.
advice: Use DOUBLE PRECISION, an 8-byte float on all four engines.

items.name: REAL
items.message: REAL keeps about 6 significant digits on PostgreSQL, against 15 on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB.

items.name: FLOAT
items.message: FLOAT keeps about 6 significant digits on MySQL and MariaDB, against 15 on SQLite and PostgreSQL.

title: CHAR(n) and trailing spaces
summary: PostgreSQL pads CHAR(n) values with spaces up to n characters; SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB give them back as stored.
detail: A CHAR(5) column holding 'a' returns 'a    ' on PostgreSQL. Comparisons there ignore the padding, so WHERE c = 'a' still matches, but the spaces reach the application and CONCAT. MySQL and MariaDB strip trailing spaces when they read CHAR values, and SQLite does not apply the length at all.
advice: Use VARCHAR(n) unless every value has exactly n characters.

title: LENGTH counts bytes on MySQL
summary: LENGTH counts characters on SQLite and PostgreSQL and bytes on MySQL and MariaDB, so LENGTH('é') is 1 or 2.
detail: In UTF-8 a letter outside A to Z takes two to four bytes. MySQL and MariaDB count characters with CHAR_LENGTH, which SQLite lacks. Length checks, cut-offs and padding drift apart on names and addresses with accents.
advice: No function counts characters on all four engines: use CHAR_LENGTH on PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB and LENGTH on SQLite.
example: SELECT LENGTH('é')

title: LOWER and UPPER outside A to Z
summary: SQLite's LOWER and UPPER change only the letters A to Z, so LOWER('ÉCOLE') is 'École' there and 'école' elsewhere.
detail: SQLite folds case for ASCII letters only, and so do its LIKE and COLLATE NOCASE, unless it is built with the ICU extension, as some systems ship it. Comparisons that use LOWER() to ignore case work on the other engines and fail on SQLite for names like Émile or Ødegaard.
advice: Fold case in the application before storing or comparing, or keep a lower-case copy of the column.
example: SELECT LOWER('ÉCOLE')

title: SUBSTR from position 0 or below
summary: SUBSTR('abc', 0, 2) is 'a' on SQLite and PostgreSQL and an empty string on MySQL and MariaDB.
detail: Positions start at 1. SQLite and PostgreSQL count position 0 as part of the requested length, while MySQL and MariaDB return nothing for a start of 0. Negative starts differ as well: SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB count them from the end, and PostgreSQL counts them before the first character.
advice: Start at 1 or later. For the last n characters, SUBSTR(x, LENGTH(x) - n + 1) works on all four for ASCII text (LENGTH counts bytes on MySQL and MariaDB).
example: SELECT SUBSTR('abc', 0, 2)
rewrite: SELECT SUBSTR('abc', 1, 1)

title: Backslashes in strings
summary: MySQL and MariaDB read a backslash in a string as an escape character; SQLite and PostgreSQL keep it as a backslash.
detail: 'C:\\temp' is C:\\temp, two backslashes, on SQLite and PostgreSQL and C:\temp on MySQL and MariaDB. '\t' is a tab and '\'' a quote there, while PostgreSQL needs its E'...' strings for escapes, which no other engine reads. MySQL's NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES mode makes it read backslashes like the others.
advice: Keep backslashes out of SQL string literals: pass such values as query parameters, which every driver sends without escaping.
example: SELECT 'C:\\temp'

items.advice: Write a quote inside a string as two quotes: 'it''s'.
items.message: \' ends the string on SQLite and PostgreSQL; only MySQL and MariaDB read it as a quote inside it.

title: Escaping % and _ in LIKE
summary: Without an ESCAPE clause, a backslash escapes % and _ in LIKE on PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB; on SQLite it is an ordinary character.
detail: 'a_b' LIKE 'a\_b' is true on PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, where \_ matches an underscore, and false on SQLite, where the pattern asks for a backslash followed by any one character.
advice: Name the escape character: LIKE 'a!_b' ESCAPE '!' means the same on all four.
example: SELECT 'a_b' LIKE 'a\_b'
rewrite: SELECT 'a_b' LIKE 'a!_b' ESCAPE '!'

title: LOG with one argument
summary: LOG(x) is the base-10 logarithm on SQLite and PostgreSQL and the natural logarithm on MySQL and MariaDB.
detail: LOG(100) is 2 on SQLite and PostgreSQL and 4.605 on MySQL and MariaDB. With two arguments, LOG(b, x) is the logarithm of x to base b on all four. SQLite has LOG, LN, LOG10 and POWER only when it is built with its math functions: the sqlite3 program is by default since version 3.35, and some systems ship it without them.
advice: Say which one you mean: LN(x) for the natural logarithm, LOG10(x) for base 10.
example: SELECT LOG(100)
rewrite: SELECT LOG10(100)

title: The ^ operator
summary: 2 ^ 3 is 8 on PostgreSQL, where ^ is a power, 1 on MySQL and MariaDB, where it is a bitwise exclusive or, and an error on SQLite.
detail: PostgreSQL raises the left side to the power of the right one. MySQL and MariaDB combine the bits of both numbers. SQLite has no ^ operator.
advice: Use POWER(a, b), which all four engines have (SQLite when it is built with its math functions).
example: SELECT 2 ^ 3
rewrite: SELECT POWER(2, 3)

title: -- comments need a space on MySQL
summary: On MySQL and MariaDB, -- starts a comment only when a space follows it, so SELECT 1 --1 is 2 there and 1 elsewhere.
detail: SQLite and PostgreSQL treat every -- as the start of a comment. MySQL and MariaDB need a space, a tab or a line break after the dashes; otherwise they are two minus signs.
advice: Put a space after --.
example: SELECT 1 --1
rewrite: SELECT 1 -- 1

title: Upper-case column names
summary: PostgreSQL lowers the case of unquoted names, so SELECT 1 AS Total returns a column named total there and Total elsewhere.
detail: SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB return names as written. PostgreSQL folds unquoted names to lower case, in aliases and in CREATE TABLE alike, so code that reads columns by name (row["Total"]) finds nothing on PostgreSQL.
advice: Use lower-case names for columns and aliases.
example: SELECT 1 AS Total
rewrite: SELECT 1 AS total

title: Table names in a different case
summary: On Linux, MySQL and MariaDB treat table names as case-sensitive, so a table created as Users is not found as users.
detail: MySQL and MariaDB keep each table in files named after it, and file names on Linux are case-sensitive (lower_case_table_names = 0, the default there). On Windows and macOS the default makes names case-insensitive. SQLite and PostgreSQL ignore case in unquoted names.
advice: Use lower-case table names and spell each one the same way everywhere.
example:
CREATE TABLE Users (id INTEGER);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users
rewrite:
CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users

title: SQLite keeps values that do not fit the column
summary: SQLite stores 'abc' in an INTEGER column and 'abcdef' in a VARCHAR(3) column; PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB refuse both.
detail: Column types on SQLite are preferences: a value that does not fit is stored as it is, and lengths are never checked. Tests that run on SQLite then pass with data the production engine rejects. SQLite's STRICT tables (version 3.37 and later) check types but not lengths, and the other engines do not accept the STRICT keyword.
advice: Run the tests on the production engine as well, or check values in the application before they reach the database.

a quoted fraction in an integer column
a fraction in an integer column
too long for VARCHAR(n)

title: Booleans and numbers
summary: PostgreSQL keeps booleans and numbers apart: active = 1, WHERE 1 and inserting 1 into a BOOLEAN column all fail there.
detail: On SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB a boolean is the number 0 or 1, and TRUE is another way to write 1. PostgreSQL has a real boolean type with no automatic conversion from integers, so code written for MySQL that compares flags with 1 stops there.
advice: Compare and insert TRUE and FALSE (active = TRUE, or simply WHERE active). All four engines accept them.
setup:
CREATE TABLE users (active BOOLEAN);
INSERT INTO users VALUES (TRUE)
example: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE active = 1
rewrite: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users WHERE active = TRUE

items.name: boolean = number
items.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (b BOOLEAN);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (TRUE)
items.probe: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t WHERE b = 1

items.name: WHERE number
items.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (b BOOLEAN);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (TRUE)
items.advice: Write a comparison: WHERE x <> 0, or WHERE 1 = 1.

items.name: number into BOOLEAN
items.advice: Insert TRUE or FALSE.

title: Numbering new rows
summary: No syntax for numbering new rows works on all four engines, and SERIAL, which works on PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, leaves the column NULL on SQLite.
detail: AUTO_INCREMENT belongs to MySQL and MariaDB, AUTOINCREMENT to SQLite, and GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY to PostgreSQL. SERIAL is PostgreSQL's as well, and MySQL and MariaDB accept it as BIGINT UNSIGNED NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT UNIQUE. SQLite accepts any type name, so SERIAL is only a name there and the column stays NULL: SQLite numbers rows for a column declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY and nothing else.
advice: No column definition numbers rows on all four engines. Keep one schema file per engine for these tables, or let the application assign the ids.

items.name: SERIAL
items.message: SERIAL numbers rows on PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB; on SQLite it is only a type name and the column stays NULL.

items.name: BIGSERIAL
items.message: {what} exists on PostgreSQL only; MySQL and MariaDB refuse it, and SQLite leaves the column NULL.

items.name: AUTO_INCREMENT
AUTOINCREMENT
GENERATED AS IDENTITY
IDENTITY(1, 1)
items.message: IDENTITY(1, 1) belongs to SQL Server: PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB refuse it, and SQLite reads it as part of the type name and leaves the column NULL.

title: Backticks around names
summary: Backticks quote names on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB; PostgreSQL refuses them.
detail: `name` is MySQL's way of quoting a name, and SQLite and MariaDB accept it too. PostgreSQL reads the backtick as a syntax error.
advice: Use plain lower-case names that are not keywords; they need no quotes on any engine.
setup:
CREATE TABLE people (name VARCHAR(20));
INSERT INTO people VALUES ('Ann')
example: SELECT `name` FROM people
rewrite: SELECT name FROM people

title: # comments
summary: # starts a comment on MySQL and MariaDB only; SQLite refuses it, and PostgreSQL reads it as the XOR operator.
detail: Scripts written for the mysql client often use # comments. SQLite stops with a syntax error. On PostgreSQL # is a bitwise exclusive or, so the rest of the line becomes part of the expression.
advice: Use -- comments, with a space after the dashes, or /* ... */.
example: SELECT 1 # one
rewrite: SELECT 1 -- one

title: NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST
summary: NULLS FIRST and NULLS LAST work on SQLite and PostgreSQL; MySQL and MariaDB refuse them.
detail: SQLite added them in version 3.30. MySQL and MariaDB have no syntax for choosing where NULL sorts.
advice: Sort on x IS NULL first: ORDER BY x IS NULL, x for NULLS LAST and ORDER BY x IS NOT NULL, x for NULLS FIRST.
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (NULL), (2)
example: SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x NULLS LAST
rewrite: SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x IS NULL, x

title: LIMIT offset, count
summary: LIMIT offset, count works on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB; PostgreSQL refuses it.
detail: In LIMIT a, b the first number is the offset and the second the count, the reverse of the order in which LIMIT ... OFFSET reads.
advice: Write LIMIT count OFFSET offset, which all four accept: LIMIT 1, 2 becomes LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1.
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (2), (3)
example: SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x LIMIT 1, 2
rewrite: SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x LIMIT 2 OFFSET 1

title: FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY
summary: The standard FETCH FIRST works on PostgreSQL and MariaDB; SQLite and MySQL refuse it.
detail: MariaDB added FETCH FIRST in version 10.6. SQLite and MySQL know only LIMIT, and they refuse OFFSET n ROWS for the same reason.
advice: Use LIMIT n, with OFFSET m when you need an offset.
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (2), (3)
example: SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY
rewrite: SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x LIMIT 2

items.name: FETCH FIRST
items.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (2), (3)
items.probe: SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x FETCH FIRST 2 ROWS ONLY

items.name: OFFSET n ROWS
items.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (2), (3)
items.probe: SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x OFFSET 1 ROWS
items.advice: Use LIMIT n OFFSET m, which all four accept.

title: Select-list names in WHERE
summary: SQLite lets WHERE use a name given in the select list; PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB refuse it.
detail: WHERE is worked out before the select list, so in standard SQL the y of SELECT x * 2 AS y does not exist yet. SQLite looks it up anyway.
advice: Repeat the expression in WHERE (WHERE x * 2 > 2), or select from a subquery that defines the name.
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (2)
example: SELECT x * 2 AS y FROM t WHERE y > 2
rewrite: SELECT x * 2 AS y FROM t WHERE x * 2 > 2

title: Select-list names in HAVING
summary: SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB let HAVING use a name given in the select list; PostgreSQL refuses it.
detail: PostgreSQL looks up names in HAVING among the table's columns only, so HAVING n > 1 fails when n is the name of COUNT(*).
advice: Repeat the aggregate: HAVING COUNT(*) > 1.
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (1), (2)
example: SELECT a, COUNT(*) AS n FROM t GROUP BY a HAVING n > 1
rewrite: SELECT a, COUNT(*) AS n FROM t GROUP BY a HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

title: LIMIT inside IN (...)
summary: MySQL and MariaDB refuse LIMIT in a subquery under IN, ANY, ALL or SOME; SQLite and PostgreSQL accept it.
detail: Both report that this version doesn't yet support 'LIMIT & IN/ALL/ANY/SOME subquery'. LIMIT is fine in a subquery used as a table and in one that returns a single value.
advice: Wrap the limited query in a subquery used as a table: IN (SELECT x FROM (SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x LIMIT 1) AS s).
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1), (2)
example: SELECT x FROM t WHERE x IN (SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x LIMIT 1)
rewrite: SELECT x FROM t WHERE x IN (SELECT x FROM (SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x LIMIT 1) AS s)

title: UPDATE or DELETE that reads its own table
summary: MySQL refuses an UPDATE or DELETE whose subquery reads the table being changed; SQLite, PostgreSQL and MariaDB accept it.
detail: MySQL says you can't specify target table 't' for update in FROM clause. MariaDB lifted the limit in version 10.3.2. A subquery used as a table works on MySQL too, because MySQL then computes its rows before it changes anything.
advice: Wrap the subquery in one more SELECT used as a table: WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT id FROM t WHERE x = 0) AS s).
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 0), (2, 5)
example:
UPDATE t SET x = 1 WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM t WHERE x = 0);
SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY id
rewrite:
UPDATE t SET x = 1 WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT id FROM t WHERE x = 0) AS s);
SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY id

title: UPDATE and DELETE with a join
summary: UPDATE ... FROM works on SQLite and PostgreSQL and UPDATE ... JOIN on MySQL and MariaDB; neither works on all four.
detail: The engines use different syntax for changing rows based on another table. DELETE differs the same way: DELETE ... USING on PostgreSQL, DELETE t FROM t JOIN ... on MySQL and MariaDB.
advice: Use subqueries, which all four accept: UPDATE t SET x = (SELECT u.x FROM u WHERE u.id = t.id) WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM u WHERE u.id = t.id), and DELETE FROM t WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM u).
example:
UPDATE t SET x = u.x FROM u WHERE u.id = t.id;
SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY id
rewrite:
UPDATE t SET x = (SELECT u.x FROM u WHERE u.id = t.id) WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM u WHERE u.id = t.id);
SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY id

items.name: UPDATE ... FROM
items.probe:
UPDATE t SET x = u.x FROM u WHERE u.id = t.id;
SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY id

items.name: UPDATE ... JOIN
items.probe:
UPDATE t JOIN u ON u.id = t.id SET t.x = u.x;
SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY id

items.name: DELETE ... JOIN
items.probe:
DELETE t FROM t JOIN u ON u.id = t.id;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t

items.name: DELETE ... USING
items.probe:
DELETE FROM t USING u WHERE u.id = t.id;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t
items.message: DELETE ... USING means one thing on PostgreSQL and another on MySQL and MariaDB, and SQLite refuses it.

title: FULL OUTER JOIN
summary: FULL OUTER JOIN works on SQLite and PostgreSQL; MySQL and MariaDB refuse it.
detail: MySQL and MariaDB have LEFT and RIGHT joins only. SQLite added RIGHT and FULL joins in version 3.39.
advice: Combine a LEFT JOIN with the rows of the other table that found no match: ... FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.x = b.x UNION ALL SELECT ... FROM b LEFT JOIN a ON a.x = b.x WHERE a.x IS NULL.
example: SELECT a.x, b.x FROM a FULL OUTER JOIN b ON a.x = b.x
rewrite: SELECT a.x, b.x FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON a.x = b.x UNION ALL SELECT a.x, b.x FROM b LEFT JOIN a ON a.x = b.x WHERE a.x IS NULL

title: DISTINCT ON
summary: DISTINCT ON (a) keeps one row per value of a on PostgreSQL only.
detail: SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB report a syntax error. Window functions say the same thing on all four (SQLite 3.25, MySQL 8.0 and MariaDB 10.2 and later).
advice: Number the rows of each group and keep the first: SELECT a, b FROM (SELECT a, b, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) AS n FROM t) AS s WHERE n = 1.
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 5), (1, 3), (2, 4)
example: SELECT DISTINCT ON (a) a, b FROM t ORDER BY a, b
rewrite: SELECT a, b FROM (SELECT a, b, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY a ORDER BY b) AS n FROM t) AS s WHERE n = 1 ORDER BY a

title: COUNT(DISTINCT a, b)
summary: COUNT(DISTINCT a, b) counts pairs on MySQL and MariaDB; SQLite and PostgreSQL take one expression only.
detail: SQLite reports the wrong number of arguments and PostgreSQL a missing function.
advice: Count the rows of a DISTINCT subquery: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT a, b FROM t) AS s.
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 1), (1, 1), (1, 2)
example: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT a, b) FROM t
rewrite: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT DISTINCT a, b FROM t) AS s

title: GREATEST and LEAST
summary: GREATEST and LEAST are missing on SQLite, skip NULL on PostgreSQL and return NULL on MySQL and MariaDB.
detail: GREATEST(1, NULL) is 1 on PostgreSQL and NULL on MySQL and MariaDB. SQLite has the same idea under the names MAX(a, b) and MIN(a, b) with two or more arguments; they return NULL when any argument is NULL, and the other engines read MAX and MIN as aggregates.
advice: Write it out with CASE and say what NULL should do. CASE WHEN a IS NULL THEN b WHEN b IS NULL OR a >= b THEN a ELSE b END skips NULL, as PostgreSQL's GREATEST does, on all four engines. A plain CASE WHEN a >= b THEN a ELSE b END answers b whenever the comparison meets a NULL, so it gives 5 for (NULL, 5) and NULL for (1, NULL).
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, a INTEGER, b INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 1, NULL), (2, NULL, 5)
example: SELECT GREATEST(a, b) FROM t ORDER BY id
rewrite: SELECT CASE WHEN a IS NULL THEN b WHEN b IS NULL OR a >= b THEN a ELSE b END FROM t ORDER BY id

title: Inserting only new rows
summary: INSERT IGNORE belongs to MySQL and MariaDB, INSERT OR IGNORE to SQLite, and ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING to PostgreSQL and SQLite.
detail: Each form skips rows that would break a unique key, and each fails on the engines that use another one. INSERT IGNORE also hides other errors on MySQL and MariaDB, such as values that do not fit the column.
advice: Insert from a SELECT that checks first: INSERT INTO t (id) SELECT 1 WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE id = 1). When two sessions insert the same row at once, the unique key still stops the second one, with an error instead of a skip.
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1)
example:
INSERT IGNORE INTO t VALUES (1);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t
rewrite:
INSERT INTO t (id) SELECT 1 WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE id = 1);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t

items.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1)
items.probe:
INSERT IGNORE INTO t VALUES (1);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t

items.name: INSERT OR IGNORE
items.setup:

INSERT INTO t VALUES (1)

items.setup:

items.probe:

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t

title: Insert or update (upsert)
summary: ON CONFLICT ... DO UPDATE works on SQLite and PostgreSQL and ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE on MySQL and MariaDB; no single statement works on all four.
detail: REPLACE INTO works on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB, but it deletes the old row and inserts a new one, which fires delete triggers and resets the columns the statement leaves out. Of these four engines, MERGE exists on PostgreSQL 15 and later only.
advice: Update first, then insert what is missing: UPDATE t SET n = 2 WHERE id = 1, then INSERT INTO t (id, n) SELECT 1, 2 WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM t WHERE id = 1). Run both in one transaction.
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, n INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 1)
example:
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 2) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET n = excluded.n;
SELECT n FROM t

items.name: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE
items.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, n INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 1)
items.probe:
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 2) ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET n = excluded.n;
SELECT n FROM t

items.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, n INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 1)
items.probe:
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 2) ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE n = 2;
SELECT n FROM t

items.name: REPLACE INTO
items.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, n INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 1)
items.probe:

items.note: It deletes the old row first, so the columns it leaves out lose their values.

items.name: MERGE

items.probe:
MERGE INTO t USING (SELECT 1 AS id, 2 AS n) s ON t.id = s.id WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET n = s.n WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT VALUES (s.id, s.n);
SELECT n FROM t

title: RETURNING
summary: INSERT ... RETURNING works on SQLite, PostgreSQL and MariaDB; MySQL refuses it.
detail: SQLite added RETURNING in version 3.35, and MariaDB in 10.5 for INSERT and DELETE (MariaDB refuses it on UPDATE). Each engine also has its own function for the last generated id: LAST_INSERT_ID() on MySQL and MariaDB, last_insert_rowid() on SQLite and lastval() on PostgreSQL.
advice: Read the new id through the driver, which has a call for it on every engine, or select the row again by a unique key after the insert.
setup: CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, x INTEGER)
example: INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 5) RETURNING id
rewrite:
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 5);
SELECT id FROM t WHERE x = 5

items.name: INSERT ... RETURNING
items.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 5)
items.probe: INSERT INTO t VALUES (2, 6) RETURNING id

items.name: UPDATE ... RETURNING
items.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 5)
items.probe: UPDATE t SET x = 6 RETURNING id

items.name: DELETE ... RETURNING
items.setup:
CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 5)

title: VARCHAR without a length
summary: VARCHAR without a length works on SQLite and PostgreSQL; MySQL and MariaDB require one.
detail: PostgreSQL reads VARCHAR without a length as text of any length, and SQLite ignores lengths anyway.
advice: Give a length, VARCHAR(255), or use TEXT for long values.
example:
CREATE TABLE t (x VARCHAR);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t
rewrite:
CREATE TABLE t (x VARCHAR(255));
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t

title: Column types that exist on some engines only
summary: Many column types belong to one or two engines: DATETIME and TINYINT are missing on PostgreSQL, BYTEA and TIMESTAMPTZ on MySQL and MariaDB.
detail: SQLite accepts nearly any type name, so a schema that works there can still fail elsewhere. Each type in the table was used in a CREATE TABLE on all four engines.
advice: Use types that all four accept: INTEGER, BIGINT, SMALLINT, DECIMAL(p, s), DOUBLE PRECISION, VARCHAR(n), TEXT, DATE, TIME, TIMESTAMP and BOOLEAN. There is no binary type they share: BLOB on SQLite, MySQL and MariaDB, BYTEA on PostgreSQL.
example:
CREATE TABLE t (d DATETIME);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t
rewrite:
CREATE TABLE t (d TIMESTAMP);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t

title: MySQL table options
summary: ENGINE=, DEFAULT CHARSET=, indexes inside CREATE TABLE, column comments and ON UPDATE belong to MySQL and MariaDB; SQLite and PostgreSQL refuse them.
detail: Dumps made with mysqldump carry these options on every table. SQLite's own options, WITHOUT ROWID and STRICT, fail on the other three engines in the same way.
advice: Leave the options out of schemas meant for every engine, and create indexes with separate CREATE INDEX statements.
example:
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER) ENGINE=InnoDB;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t
rewrite:
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t

title: DEFAULT on TEXT columns
summary: MySQL refuses a plain DEFAULT value on TEXT, BLOB and JSON columns; SQLite, PostgreSQL and MariaDB accept it.
detail: MySQL 8.0.13 and later accept a default written as an expression in parentheses, DEFAULT ('a'), which the other three engines accept as well.
advice: Put the default in parentheses, DEFAULT ('a'), or use VARCHAR(n).

title: Keys on TEXT columns
summary: MySQL refuses an index, unique key or primary key on a TEXT or BLOB column without a prefix length, and MariaDB refuses the primary key.
detail: SQLite and PostgreSQL index TEXT columns as they are. MySQL wants a prefix length, INDEX (x(100)), which the others reject. MariaDB 10.4 and later accept plain indexes and unique keys on TEXT columns.
advice: Use VARCHAR(n) for columns you index.
example:
CREATE TABLE t (x TEXT PRIMARY KEY);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t
rewrite:
CREATE TABLE t (x VARCHAR(255) PRIMARY KEY);
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t

title: CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS
summary: MySQL refuses IF NOT EXISTS in CREATE INDEX; SQLite, PostgreSQL and MariaDB accept it.
detail: MySQL accepts IF NOT EXISTS for tables and databases, and not for indexes.
advice: Create each index once, in a migration that runs once, without IF NOT EXISTS.

title: TRUNCATE
summary: SQLite has no TRUNCATE; PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB have it.
detail: SQLite empties a table quickly with a DELETE FROM t that has no WHERE clause. On MySQL and MariaDB, TRUNCATE also resets the AUTO_INCREMENT counter, which DELETE leaves alone.
advice: Use DELETE FROM t.
setup:
CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER);
INSERT INTO t VALUES (1)
example:
TRUNCATE TABLE t;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t
rewrite:
DELETE FROM t;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t

title: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW
summary: SQLite has no CREATE OR REPLACE; PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB accept it for views.
detail: SQLite can only drop a view and create it again.
advice: Drop and create: DROP VIEW IF EXISTS v, then CREATE VIEW v AS ...
setup: CREATE TABLE t (x INTEGER)
example:
CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW v AS SELECT x FROM t;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM v

title: Functions that exist on some engines only
summary: Many everyday functions are missing on at least one engine: IFNULL on PostgreSQL, LEFT and NOW on SQLite, STRING_AGG on MySQL and MariaDB.
detail: Each function in the table was called on all four engines, and the table shows where the call ran and what to write instead.
advice: Prefer the functions all four engines have: COALESCE, NULLIF, CASE, SUBSTR, REPLACE, TRIM, UPPER, LOWER, ABS, ROUND, and CONCAT (SQLite from 3.44).
example: SELECT IFNULL(NULL, 'x')
rewrite: SELECT COALESCE(NULL, 'x')

title: Operators that exist on some engines only
summary: Operators such as ::, ILIKE, DIV and <=> belong to one or two engines and are syntax errors on the others.
detail: Each operator in the table was used on all four engines, and the table shows where it ran and what to write instead.
advice: Prefer the operators all four share: = <> < > <= >= + - * / %, LIKE, IN, BETWEEN, IS NULL. Leave || out: it joins text on SQLite and PostgreSQL and means OR on MySQL and MariaDB (see pipes-concat).
example: SELECT 'abc' ILIKE 'ABC'
rewrite: SELECT LOWER('abc') LIKE LOWER('ABC')

items.advice: Use CAST(x AS type) (see cast-to-number for integers).

items.name: ILIKE
items.advice: Use LOWER(x) LIKE LOWER(pattern).

items.name: DIV
items.advice: Use (a - a % b) / b for a whole-number result.

items.name: MOD
items.advice: Use a % b.
Use (a = b OR (a IS NULL AND b IS NULL)).

items.name: REGEXP
items.advice: No form works on all four engines; ~ on PostgreSQL; REGEXP works in SQLite's shell, not in every SQLite build.

items.name: RLIKE
items.advice: No form works on all four engines; ~ on PostgreSQL.
No form works on all four engines; REGEXP on MySQL and MariaDB.

items.name: SIMILAR TO
items.advice: Use LIKE where the pattern allows it.

items.name: IS DISTINCT FROM
items.advice: Use (a <> b OR (a IS NULL) <> (b IS NULL)), or <=> on MySQL and MariaDB.

items.name: XOR
items.advice: Use (a OR b) AND NOT (a AND b).
Use AND.

items.name: GLOB
items.advice: Use LIKE, with % for * and _ for ?.
Use =.
Use NOT.
No form works on all four engines; JSON paths and types differ on every engine.
